name: Ivan Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a maintenance crew covering a valley up in the hills, about forty kilometres of line between the dam and the last village. We meet at the substation at half six, and these days I'm the one who pulls up the fault reports on the tablet because the others hate it. Then it's driving the access tracks, checking poles, swapping insulators, cutting back trees that have grown into the line. I'm still the junior, so I'm on the ground or in the bucket with someone watching, but I'm getting there.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You're the tablet person on the crew. Where does that come from, and what's hard about the job for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I spent fifteen years installing broadband and TV boxes, so screens don't scare me. That company got bought and they cut the installers to contractors on piece rates, and I said no thanks. The hard part here is the physical feel of it, knowing by instinct what a line is doing, which the old guys have and I don't yet. And honestly the money, apprentice pay with a mortgage and Giulia doing night shifts at the hospital, we're always a couple of weeks from the edge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fair enough, it's a tool, not a miracle, which is what I've been saying to the lads anyway. Online I'd probably post something like, good, now let's talk about who got the savings from the bit it did automate. I'm in a couple of union groups and that's the kind of thing we argue about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, nothing much changes. I keep using it to study, I finish my apprenticeship, the job's still here. Money's still tight, but that was never about AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. I'd keep going on the apprenticeship, keep using the chat apps to quiz myself for the electrical theory exams, and keep pushing the union on apprentice pay. Maybe I'd try to grab some overtime in the winter storms to get a little cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. Maybe a touch bored.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you use AI day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every day. I ask it to explain things in the manuals that I didn't get, I make it quiz me on clearance distances, and I use it to check the fault reports against the maps. Last month it helped me write a proper complaint to the council about a lorry park under a line, and they actually fixed it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you be disappointed, in a way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yeah. I like new things. But for my family, steady is good. Giulia would be thrilled if nothing changed except my pay going up.

S0.say: He'd say AI is a tool, not a miracle, which he already tells the crew. Online he'd ask who got the savings from the parts it did automate.
S0.think: Nothing much changes for me. I keep using AI to study, finish my apprenticeship, and money stays tight, which was never about AI.
S0.do: Carries on with his apprenticeship, using chat apps to quiz himself for the electrical theory exams. Pushes the union on apprentice pay and picks up winter storm overtime to build a small cushion.
S0.feel: Calm, a touch bored, and fine with steady for his family's sake.
S0.quote: I make it quiz me on clearance distances, and I use it to check the fault reports against the maps.
S0.fieldNote: Ivan is the one daily AI user on a crew that dislikes screens, a habit from fifteen years installing broadband. He'd be slightly disappointed by a plateau but knows steady suits his family. His money worries are separate from AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good if it's done right, and the union needs to make sure it's done right. At work I'd tell the crew it's going to be drones and sensors, so let's be the ones who run them. Online I'd be arguing that the productivity gains should go into wages and shorter weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'd do well. I'm the one who already knows the tablet, so I'd be the one they send on the drone course. The risk is the money, because if they cut hours during the change, I have nothing to fall back on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ask the supervisor straight away about the drone inspection course, and get on it within six months if the company pays. Use AI tools to learn the new fault-detection software before it arrives. And at the union, push for a deal where nobody loses hours during retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, actually. Excited, with a little worry about the bills underneath.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you see this as a chance or a threat for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A chance. I came to this job at forty, I'll never be the best climber on the crew. But I could be the best at the new stuff, and that's a way up that didn't exist before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the older guys on the crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lou, who's sixty and won't touch a phone, I worry about. He knows more about lines than anyone, and if they push him out for not reading a tablet, that's a crime. I'd want to pair up with him, he teaches me the feel, I help him with the screens.

S1.say: He'd say the change is good if done right and the union must make sure it is. He'd tell the crew to be the ones who run the drones and sensors, and argue online that gains should go to wages and shorter weeks.
S1.think: I'd do well, because I already know the tablet and they'd send me on the drone course. The risk is money, if hours get cut during the change.
S1.do: Asks his supervisor about a company-paid drone inspection course and aims to be on it within six months. Uses AI to learn the new fault-detection software early and pushes the union for no lost hours during retraining.
S1.feel: Excited, with a thin layer of worry about bills underneath.
S1.quote: I'll never be the best climber on the crew. But I could be the best at the new stuff, and that's a way up that didn't exist before.
S1.fieldNote: For Ivan, gradual change opens a ladder that his late start had closed. He pairs ambition with solidarity, worrying about the senior lineman Lou and proposing a skills swap. His only fear is cash flow during a transition.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for a universal basic income, a payment everyone gets just for being a citizen, and public ownership of the robots that run the grid. At the depot I'd say we stick together. Online I'd be loud, honestly, angrier than I usually am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, being good with tech doesn't save me if the tech is doing my job. Two years means I don't even finish the apprenticeship, and there's no robot-running job for an unqualified guy when the robot runs itself. We'd have maybe three weeks before things get serious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd try to become the person who installs and maintains whatever robots they bring in, because someone has to for a while. I'd sell Giulia's car, we can manage on one, which is a few thousand. I'd be at every union action, and I'd push hard on the politics side, because this has to be a public decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. Really scared, in a way I haven't felt since we lost our first pregnancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're used to being ahead of change. Does that help here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, because I'd see it coming a few months before the others. But it's like being the first to see a wave, you still get wet. I'd use the head start to grab whatever bridge job exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The second car, then the kids' football fees, then probably the internet, which is ironic for an old broadband guy. Luca's thirteen and he'd notice. Sofia wouldn't, she just wants to know if the dog's coming with us wherever we go.

S2.say: He'd call for a universal basic income and public ownership of the robots that run the grid, tell the crew to stick together, and be louder online than usual.
S2.think: Being good with tech doesn't save me if the tech does my job. I wouldn't finish my apprenticeship, there's no job for an unqualified robot minder, and we'd have about three weeks of cash.
S2.do: Tries in the first month to become the person installing and maintaining the new robots. Sells his partner's car for a few thousand and joins every union action while pushing for public control.
S2.feel: Really scared, more than he has been in years.
S2.quote: It's like being the first to see a wave, you still get wet.
S2.fieldNote: Ivan's usual confidence breaks here: his tech skills don't help if the tech replaces the job, and his savings are only weeks deep. He still moves first, chasing a bridge job installing robots. His politics sharpen into calls for basic income and public ownership.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years to decide who owns this, and if we waste them we deserve what we get. At the union I'd be pushing for a transition fund. With friends I'd say learn the machines now, don't wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I finish my ticket and I get in early on the robot side. I think I'd have three or four good years being the guy who helps install and fix them. After 2031 I don't know, but I'd have more choices and maybe a bit saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get qualified in two or three years, take every robotics or automation course I can, starting with online ones this winter. Put a hundred a month aside, even if it means fewer takeaways. And I'd try to get onto the company team that tests new kit, so I'm on the inside when it arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more in charge of it. Like having time to pack before a storm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years let you do that two doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is a crash. Five years is a race, and I'm a decent runner. I'd still be worried about the end, but I'd be running toward something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Giulia's job be safer than yours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe for a while. Nurses deal with people at their worst, and I don't think families want a robot doing that. But her hospital's already using AI for rotas and notes, so she's not untouched either.

S3.say: He'd say there are five years to decide who owns the technology, push the union for a transition fund, and tell friends to learn the machines now.
S3.think: Five years means I finish my ticket and get in early on the robot side, with three or four good years installing and fixing them. After 2031 I don't know, but I'd have more choices.
S3.do: Qualifies within two or three years and takes every robotics or automation course he can, starting online this winter. Saves 100 a month by cutting takeaways and tries to join the company team that tests new kit.
S3.feel: Anxious but more in charge, like having time to pack before a storm.
S3.quote: Two years is a crash. Five years is a race, and I'm a decent runner.
S3.fieldNote: The extra three years turn Ivan's fear into a race he thinks he can run. He'd use AI and online courses to get onto the company's testing team. He's honest that he can't see past 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to build a fair system, a shorter week, public ownership of the grid robots, retraining paid for by the companies that profit. I'd be campaigning for it, properly. I'd tell friends this is a political fight, not a tech story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, ten years is a decent runway. I'd be qualified, I'd have learned the robot side, and I'd probably move into training or managing the machines. I'm more worried about whether the gains get shared than about myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Finish the apprenticeship, then aim for a supervisor or technician role on the automated crews within five years. Start studying engineering part-time, maybe through the union's education fund. And get involved in local politics, maybe run for something on the council.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but hopeful. It's the most hopeful I'd be about any of these.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for Luca and Sofia?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want them to learn to think, to argue, to care for people. Luca loves building things, so maybe engineering. Sofia's eight, she just wants to be a vet this week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you worry about anyone else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lou and the other old guys, and the people in the villages who already pay too much for power. If robots make it cheaper, that should show up on their bills, not just in shareholders' pockets. That's what I'd be fighting for.

S4.say: He'd say ten years is enough to build a fair system with a shorter week, public ownership of the grid robots and company-funded retraining, and he'd campaign for it as a political fight.
S4.think: Ten years is a decent runway: qualified, trained on the robot side, probably training others or managing machines. I'm more worried about whether the gains get shared than about myself.
S4.do: Finishes his apprenticeship and aims for a technician or supervisor role on automated crews within five years. Starts part-time engineering study through the union education fund and gets involved in local politics, possibly standing for council.
S4.feel: Uneasy but hopeful, the most hopeful of the five.
S4.quote: If robots make it cheaper, that should show up on their bills, not just in shareholders' pockets.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Ivan's concern turns outward to the older linemen and village households. He sees a career path for himself and wants to run for local office. His progressive politics and his love of new tech line up here.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Not because I can't learn, but because there's no time to learn and no money to fall back on. What would help is a basic income floor, so my family doesn't fall through while I retrain, and the union having a real seat at the table about how the robots come in.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who decides. Everyone asks if people will lose their jobs, nobody asks who gets to say how the machines are used. I put cable in half the houses in my old town, and I never got a vote on anything. I'd like a vote this time.

headlineQuote: I put cable in half the houses in my old town, and I never got a vote on anything. I'd like a vote this time.
portrait: Ivan Rossi is a 43-year-old apprentice lineworker on a hill-valley maintenance crew, who spent fifteen years installing broadband before the job was turned into piece-rate contracting. He uses AI every day to study and check fault reports, and he's the crew's tablet person. His partner Giulia is a night-shift nurse, they have two kids, and they live a couple of weeks from the edge. He is calm through the plateau and gradual change, which he sees as a ladder up, alarmed when AGI arrives in two years, and treats five and ten years as a race he can run, with his politics focused on who owns the machines.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because there'd be no time to learn and no money to fall back on.
whatWouldHelp: A basic income floor so his family doesn't fall through while he retrains, and a real seat for the union in deciding how robots come in.
